transcript.heading: News Report One (British Male)
paras: A new report from the World Health Organization has found that air pollution is responsible for approximately seven million premature deaths every year worldwide, making it one of the leading environmental health risks of our time. The report states that 99 percent of the global population breathes air that exceeds WHO guideline limits for safe air quality, with the highest levels of pollution found in low- and middle-income countries, particularly in South Asia and Africa. The main sources of air pollution include vehicle emissions, industrial processes, household burning of fuels for cooking and heating, and agricultural activities. Fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, is especially dangerous because these tiny particles can enter deep into the lungs and bloodstream, causing heart disease, stroke, lung cancer, and respiratory infections. The WHO is calling on governments to take urgent action to reduce air pollution by investing in clean energy, improving public transportation, reducing industrial emissions, and promoting cleaner cooking methods for households. They say that even small reductions in air pollution can have significant health benefits and save millions of lives.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Female)
paras: A school district in Oregon has become the first in the United States to adopt a four-day school week for all of its schools, with students attending classes Monday through Thursday and having Fridays off. The change, which began this semester, was implemented to help recruit and retain teachers amid a nationwide teacher shortage, as well as to give students more time for rest, extracurricular activities, and family time. The school day has been slightly longer on the four days to make up for the lost day, so total instructional time remains the same as before. Early feedback from teachers, students, and parents has been mostly positive. Teachers say they have more time to prepare lessons and grade papers, while students report feeling less stressed and having more time to pursue hobbies, work part-time jobs, or spend time with family. Some parents, however, have expressed concerns about finding childcare for their children on Fridays, especially for younger kids. The school district says it will monitor the results carefully over the next two years and may adjust the schedule if needed. Several other school districts around the country are considering similar changes.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Researchers at the University of Chicago have developed an artificial intelligence system that can detect early signs of pancreatic cancer from routine blood tests, potentially catching the disease years before it would normally be diagnosed. Pancreatic cancer is one of the deadliest forms of cancer, with a five-year survival rate of only about 12 percent, largely because it is usually detected at a late stage when symptoms appear and treatment options are limited. The AI algorithm works by analyzing patterns in common blood test results that are too subtle for human doctors to notice, identifying patients who are at high risk of developing pancreatic cancer within the next one to three years. In testing, the system was able to correctly identify about 90 percent of patients who would go on to develop the disease, while producing relatively few false positives. Researchers say the technology could be especially useful because it uses data from blood tests that most people already get during regular checkups, meaning it could be implemented widely without requiring expensive new screening procedures. The team is now working on larger clinical trials to validate the results before the system can be approved for clinical use.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (David): Hey Maria, I saw you at the gym earlier—you were really going hard on the treadmill. Are you training for something?
Woman (Maria): Oh hey David. Yeah, I'm training for a half marathon next month. It's my first one, so I'm kind of nervous about it.
Man: A half marathon? That's 13 miles, right? Wow, that's impressive. How long have you been running?
Woman: Well, I only started running seriously about six months ago. Before that, I could barely run a mile without stopping. I've been building up slowly—adding a little more distance each week.
Man: That's smart—you don't want to push too hard too fast and get injured. What made you decide to run a half marathon?

Woman: Honestly, I was feeling really out of shape and unhealthy last year, and I wanted to set a big goal to motivate myself. I've always admired people who run marathons, and I thought a half marathon would be a good challenge without being completely impossible. Plus, I'm raising money for charity—my mom has diabetes, so I'm running for the American Diabetes Association.
Man: That's really cool. How's the training going? Are you feeling ready?

Woman: It's going okay, but it's definitely harder than I expected. Some weeks I feel great and can run long distances no problem, and other weeks my legs feel heavy and I can barely finish my runs. And I'm always so hungry— I feel like I'm eating constantly.
Man: Yeah, that's normal. When you're training for long distances, your body needs a lot of fuel. Are you doing any other training besides running? Like strength training or cross-training?

Woman: I know I should be, but I haven't really had time. I'm so busy with work and then running takes up so much of my free time. But I've heard that strength training can help prevent injuries, right?

Man: Definitely. It helps strengthen your muscles and joints, which makes you less likely to get hurt. Even just 20 or 30 minutes a couple times a week makes a big difference. What about your shoes—do you have good running shoes?
Woman: I think so? I just bought some new ones a couple months ago. But I'm not sure if they're the right kind for my feet or my running style.

Man: Oh, you should definitely go to a specialty running store and get fitted properly. They can watch you run and recommend the right shoes for you. Wearing the wrong shoes is one of the most common causes of running injuries.
Woman: Really? I had no idea. I just bought a pair that looked nice and felt comfortable in the store.

Man: Yeah, that's what a lot of people do. But everyone's feet are different, and the right shoes can make a huge difference. If you want, I can go with you to the running store near my apartment—they're really good there.
Woman: That would be great! Thanks, David. I really appreciate all the advice. I'm still pretty new to this running thing.
Man: No problem. It's always better to learn from someone else's mistakes than make them all yourself. Let me know when you're free and we can go.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: The history of chocolate is a long and fascinating one that spans thousands of years and multiple continents. The story of chocolate begins in ancient Mesoamerica, where the Olmec, Maya, and Aztec civilizations cultivated cacao trees and used cacao beans to make a bitter, frothy drink that was consumed for both ceremonial and medicinal purposes.

The Maya, who lived in what is now southern Mexico and Central America, were growing cacao as early as 600 AD. They considered cacao a gift from the gods, and cacao beans were used as currency, as offerings in religious ceremonies, and even as medicine for various ailments. The chocolate drink they made was very different from the sweet chocolate we know today—it was made by grinding roasted cacao beans with water, chili peppers, cornmeal, and other spices, and it was served unsweetened and often frothy.

When the Spanish arrived in the Americas in the 16th century, they were initially unimpressed with chocolate, finding it bitter and strange-tasting. But they soon developed a taste for it, especially after they started adding sugar and cinnamon to make it sweeter. Chocolate became a fashionable drink among the Spanish aristocracy, and it was kept a secret from the rest of Europe for nearly a hundred years before it spread to other countries.

By the 17th century, chocolate houses—similar to coffee houses—were popular in London, Paris, and other European cities, where wealthy people gathered to drink chocolate and socialize. But chocolate was still very expensive and only available to the upper classes, because cacao had to be imported from the Americas and the production process was labor-intensive.

The Industrial Revolution changed all of that. In the 19th century, new inventions like the cocoa press and the conching machine made it possible to produce chocolate cheaper and in larger quantities, and to create solid chocolate bars instead of just a drink. Companies like Cadbury in England and Nestlé in Switzerland began mass-producing chocolate, making it affordable for ordinary people for the first time.

Today, chocolate is one of the most popular foods in the world, with global consumption of over 7 million tons per year. It comes in countless varieties, from dark chocolate to milk chocolate to white chocolate, and it's used in everything from candy bars and desserts to savory dishes and beverages. While we often think of chocolate as a simple treat, its long and complex history tells a story of cultural exchange, technological innovation, and global trade that spans thousands of years.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: Dreaming is a universal human experience—we all spend about two hours every night dreaming, even if we don't remember our dreams when we wake up. But despite thousands of years of curiosity and research, scientists still don't fully understand why we dream or what purpose dreams serve. There are, however, several major theories that attempt to explain this mysterious phenomenon.

One of the most famous theories comes from Sigmund Freud, the founder of psychoanalysis, who argued in the late 19th century that dreams are a window into the unconscious mind, revealing our hidden desires, fears, and conflicts that we can't acknowledge while we're awake. According to Freud, the bizarre and illogical nature of dreams is because the true, often unacceptable meaning of the dream is disguised in symbolic form to protect us from the anxiety of confronting it directly. While Freud's specific ideas about dream interpretation are largely rejected by modern scientists, his theory that dreams reflect inner psychological states continues to influence how many people think about dreams.

Another theory, known as the activation-synthesis theory, proposes that dreams are actually just the brain's attempt to make sense of random neural activity that occurs during sleep. According to this theory, during REM (rapid eye movement) sleep, when most dreaming occurs, the brain stem sends random signals to the cortex, which then tries to create a story or narrative out of these random signals, resulting in the strange, disjointed quality of many dreams. In this view, dreams don't have any inherent meaning—they're just the brain making the best it can out of noise.

More recent theories focus on the role of dreaming in memory consolidation and learning. Research has shown that people who sleep after learning something new remember it better than people who stay awake, and that dreaming about the task or material is associated with even better memory. According to these theories, dreaming is part of the brain's process of sorting through the day's experiences, storing important memories, and discarding unimportant information. Dreams may also help us process emotions and prepare for future challenges by simulating possible scenarios.

The truth is, none of these theories has been proven definitively, and it's possible that dreams serve multiple purposes rather than just one. What we do know is that dreaming is essential for mental and emotional health—people who are deprived of REM sleep and dreaming experience increased anxiety, irritability, difficulty concentrating, and even hallucinations. Whatever their purpose, dreams are a fundamental part of being human.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: Volunteering—giving your time and energy to help others without being paid—has long been considered a noble and selfless act. But research has shown that volunteering doesn't just help the people and organizations you're helping—it also provides significant benefits for the volunteers themselves, both physically and mentally.

One of the most well-documented benefits of volunteering is improved mental health. Studies have consistently found that people who volunteer regularly report lower levels of stress, depression, and anxiety, and higher levels of life satisfaction and happiness. There are several reasons for this. Volunteering provides a sense of purpose and meaning, giving people something outside of themselves to focus on. It also creates social connections and builds community, reducing feelings of loneliness and isolation. And helping others activates the reward centers in the brain, releasing endorphins and creating a sense of well-being sometimes called the "helper's high."

Physical health benefits have also been found. Research shows that people who volunteer have lower blood pressure, lower risk of heart disease, and even longer lifespans compared to people who don't volunteer. This may be partly because volunteering often involves physical activity, especially for hands-on volunteer work like building houses, gardening, or walking dogs at an animal shelter. But even sedentary volunteer work like tutoring or answering phones has been linked to better health outcomes, suggesting that the social and psychological benefits also have physical effects.

Volunteering can also provide professional benefits. It gives people the opportunity to develop new skills, gain work experience, and build their professional networks. For people who are unemployed or looking to change careers, volunteering can be a way to fill gaps in their resume, learn new skills, and make connections that can lead to job opportunities. Even for people who are happy in their careers, volunteering can help develop leadership skills, teamwork abilities, and other transferable skills that are valuable in the workplace.

Interestingly, research has found that the benefits of volunteering are strongest when people choose to volunteer for reasons that are intrinsically motivating—because they care about the cause and want to help—rather than for external reasons like college applications or resume building. People who volunteer because they genuinely want to tend to get more out of the experience than people who feel forced or obligated to do it.

Of course, it's important not to overdo it—volunteering too much can actually increase stress and burnout, just like any other activity. But for most people, regular volunteering in moderation is a win-win: you get to help make a difference in your community, and you get healthier and happier in the process.
